title: Do Visual Features Improve Other-Initiated Repair Detection? A Dyadic Multimodal Approach
one_sentence: Conversation-Analysis-grounded gaze, face, head, body, and gesture features improve other-initiated-repair detection and type classification across two human-human corpora, but detection is not successful agent repair.
problem: Do visual behaviors improve automatic detection and classification of other-initiated repair, and do useful cues differ across language and interaction setting?
method: A hierarchical text-audio-visual classifier is evaluated with session-level five-fold cross-validation on French screen-mediated NOXI (47 OIR instances in seven hours) and Dutch face-to-face task-oriented CABB-S (378 instances in eight hours). Handcrafted, Conversation-Analysis-grounded visual features cover both participants' gaze, facial action units, head, body, holds, gesture, and dyadic coordination.
findings: Adding visual features to text and audio increased detection macro-F1 by 4.1 points on NOXI and 12.9 points on CABB-S.
For repair-type classification, visual features added 13.2 points on NOXI but only 2.4 points on CABB-S, indicating strong setting dependence.
NOXI estimates were unstable because OIR instances and restricted offers were sparse; visual-only features lacked sufficient specificity.
real_contribution: Supplies a multimodal, interaction-theory-grounded detector for visible trouble signals and distinguishes detection from repair-type classification across two interaction ecologies.
biggest_weakness: Both corpora are human-human, one contains only 47 repair instances, feature availability differs by corpus, and the study does not test real-time conversational-agent deployment, repair production, or downstream grounding outcomes.
claim_boundary: Supports multimodal detection of human OIR signals in two corpora; it does not show that an agent can choose, execute, or learn an effective repair policy or build common ground.
why_researcher_should_care: It fills a missing measurement component for AMSC's repair stage and shows that the informative visual channel depends on interaction setting, making single-modality repair benchmarks inadequate.
evidence_notes: Recovered when the ICMI 2026 official sessions page surfaced; full arXiv HTML and DOI metadata were inspected.
Human-human signal detection is not encoded as evidence of successful human-agent repair.
